## Ethics Thread

- Ethical issues are **not an afterthought** — they are woven throughout every week
- Core themes: **bias, fairness, privacy, exposure, transparency, stakeholder impact**
- Recommendation systems shape everyday decisions: what people read, watch, buy, apply for

::: {.callout-warning}
These systems encode values and trade-offs. Understanding how they work means understanding what they optimise for — and at whose expense.
:::

# 04 Types of Recommendation Systems {background-color="#EF7C00"}

<!-- ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     SLIDE TYPE 7 — Two-Column Layout
     ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ -->

## A Card-Suit Framework for User Types

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
♠ **Spades — The Explorer**
- Seeks novelty and diversity
- Values serendipitous discovery

♥ **Hearts — The Social Connector**
- Influenced by friends and community
- Trusts collaborative signals
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
♦ **Diamonds — The Pragmatist**
- Goal-oriented, task-driven
- Values precision over diversity

♣ **Clubs — The Loyalist**
- Sticks to known preferences
- Values consistency and familiarity
:::
:::

::: notes
<!-- TODO (students): How did Min introduce this framework? -->
:::

<!-- ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     SLIDE TYPE 8 — Incremental Bullet List
     ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════     ═�══ -->

## Classical Recommendation Paradigms

::: {.incremental}
- **Popularity-based:** Recommend globally popular items — no personalisation
- **Content-based filtering:** Items similar to what the user has liked, based on item features
- **Collaborative filtering (CF):** Leverage patterns across many users — no item features needed
- **Hybrid approaches:** Combine multiple signals for robustness
:::

::: notes
<!-- TODO (students): What specific examples or datasets did Min use? -->
:::

<!-- ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     SLIDE TYPE 9 — Blockquote
     ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ -->

## What Is a Recommendation?

> A recommendation system infers a user's latent preferences from observed behaviour and surfaces items the user is likely to value — items they would not have found on their own.

- **Latent preferences** — we never observe preferences directly; we infer them
- **Observed behaviour** — clicks, ratings, purchases, dwell time
- **Counterfactual value** — items they would not have found unaided

::: notes
The blockquote anchors the lecture vocabulary before introducing the paradigms.
:::

## 🤞 Key Point {background-color="#003D7C"}

<u>**Recommendation objectives shape who gets exposure.**</u>

Optimising purely for engagement creates a feedback loop: popular items attract more clicks, which generates more training signal, which makes them even more likely to be recommended.

Long-tail items, niche creators, and new entrants bear the cost of this loop — not the platform.

::: notes
Key Point slide. Pause here before the Ethics Thread slide.
:::

<!-- ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     SLIDE TYPE 13 — Ethics Thread (content + callout-warning)
     ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ -->

## Ethics Thread: Popularity Bias and Exposure Inequality

- Popular items get recommended → more interactions → even more popular (**feedback loop**)
- Long-tail items receive little to no exposure
- Who bears the cost? **Niche creators, minority preferences, new entrants**

::: {.callout-warning}
Recommendation objectives that optimise purely for engagement can systematically disadvantage underrepresented content.
:::

## {background-color="#002a26"}

```{=html}

    Next week we move from explicit item features to <strong style="color:#80cbc4;">learned representations</strong>.

    <br><br>
    <strong style="color:#EF7C00;">Key ideas coming up:</strong>
    <ul style="margin-top:0.5em;line-height:1.7;">

      <li><strong>Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR)</strong> — optimise for relative preference, not absolute rating</li>
      <li><strong>Implicit vs explicit feedback</strong> — what clicks, views, and skips tell us that ratings do not</li>
    </ul>
```
